title: U.S. Builds Up Middle East Presence as Post-Midterm Escalation with Iran Looms
snippet: Military deployments and political calculations suggest the U.S. may resume heavy air strikes against Iran following the November 3 elections, though analysts warn military options remain limited.
content:
WASHINGTON — The United States appears to be positioning forces for a renewed wave of major military operations against Iran following the upcoming midterm elections, according to foreign policy experts, even as strategic military solutions remain out of reach for both sides.

In recent weeks, U.S. and Iranian forces have settled into a grinding stalemate defined by low-level maritime engagements. Washington has focused on enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Tehran has sought to assert dominance over the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway. Neither country has launched major attacks against land-based targets since early September, but indicators suggest that operational pause may soon end.

Post-Election Escalation

"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to the November 3 U.S. elections.

Maloney pointed to a series of escalating signals, including the movement of additional U.S. military personnel and naval assets to the Middle East, official safety advisories issued to Americans in the region, and heightened readiness among Israeli forces. President Donald Trump recently stated publicly that he would not order new major strikes before Election Day, a move analysts view as a political calculation given how rising fuel costs linked to the conflict have dragged on Republican poll numbers.

However, Maloney noted that the status quo is unsustainable. While the U.S. blockade is inflicting economic pain on Tehran, it is also tying up a substantial portion of the U.S. Navy's operational capacity.

Expanding Forces and Strategic Limits

Military movements suggest Washington is preparing for multiple contingencies. The defense footprint could soon see the deployment of the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt, potentially bringing the total number of U.S. carrier strike groups in the region to three, alongside an additional Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, noted that Israeli combat aircraft recently conducted show-of-force exercises mimicking previous long-range strikes on Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also held high-level consultations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem.

Despite the show of force, Campbell cautioned that Washington's operational choices are far more constrained than earlier in the campaign. Strategic damage to regional host bases has made large-scale ground actions virtually impossible to execute.

"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands—in some scenarios tens of thousands—of forces that would be required for such an operation," Campbell said.

No Clear Path to Resolution

With conventional Iranian military installations largely degraded from earlier air campaigns, analysts warn that future U.S. strikes may shift toward critical infrastructure impacting the broader Iranian population. Yet, experts agree that further military action is unlikely to force Tehran into concessions.

"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.

Campbell echoed the sentiment, noting that Tehran has demonstrated a clear resolve to absorb physical damage. "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime," he said.
